```{r set_options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(phylograftR)
```

Grafting can be constrained by **species attributes** described by **stochastic character maps** (`simmap`) of the backbone phylogeny.
This tutorial explains how to use **biogeographic ranges** as attributes, i.e., **geographically-informed grafting**: a missing taxon is only grafted on the branches where its lineage could have lived in **its known range**.
A range is a **set of areas** (e.g., `"A"`, `"AB"`), and the stochastic map shows how the range of the lineages **evolved** along the backbone (e.g., from a `BioGeoBEARS` analysis).

The key is the argument `treat_states_as_ranges`, which tells the grafting functions **how to match the allowed ranges of a taxon with the ranges of the map**:

1. **Exact matching** (`treat_states_as_ranges = FALSE`, the default): ranges are unrelated states, like for categorical traits (e.g., colors). A taxon allowed in `"A"` can only be grafted on branch pieces where the map is **exactly** in `"A"`.
2. **Range matching** (`treat_states_as_ranges = TRUE`): a taxon allowed in `"A"` can be grafted wherever the lineage **includes the area `"A"`**: `"A"`, `"AB"`, `"ABC"`, etc.

We compare the two options **side by side**, with the **same data**, so that the differences shown come from the **matching type** argument (`treat_states_as_ranges`).

**Other types of data**

The principle of species attribute-based constraints is the same for all the types of data. 
For examples addressing different data types, please refer to:

- **categorical traits** (single trait): `vignette("main_workflow")`, and the examples of `vignette("graft_missing_taxa")`, `vignette("graft_missing_clades")` and `vignette("combine_missing_taxa_and_clades")`;
- **several traits** at once (or a trait and ranges): `vignette("multiple_traits")`;
- **continuous traits**: `vignette("continuous_data")`;
- **several stochastic maps** to account for the uncertainty in the evolutionary history: `vignette("handle_uncertainty")`.

To build stochastic maps of ranges from your own data, see `vignette("prepare_stochastic_maps")`.

## 0/ Data

We use the toy backbone, and the toy stochastic map of **four ranges** built from **three areas** (`"A"`, `"B"`, `"C"`): `"A"`, `"B"`, `"AB"` and `"BC"`.

```{r data, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
# ------ Toy data ------ #

data(toy_backbone)
data(toy_simmap_ranges)
data(toy_missing_taxa_list_with_allowed_ranges)

# Plot the stochastic map of ranges
range_colors <- c(A = "gold", B = "dodgerblue", AB = "limegreen", BC = "firebrick2")
phytools::plotSimmap(toy_simmap_ranges, colors = range_colors, fsize = 0.6, ftype = "i", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = names(range_colors), fill = range_colors, title = "Range", bty = "n")

# Time spent in each range, summed on all the branches
round(colSums(toy_simmap_ranges$mapped.edge))
```

**Ranges must be coded as in `BioGeoBEARS`**: one capital letter per area, and the letters of a multi-area range in alphabetical order (`"AB"`, not `"BA"`).

The list of missing taxa has the usual structure (see `vignette("format_inputs")`), with **allowed ranges** in the `allowed_states` item.
Some taxa have their own allowed ranges, the others have `NULL` and use the **global** `allowed_states` argument of the grafting function:

```{r list}
# Load missing taxa list with the allowed ranges of the 7 missing taxa
taxa_ranges <- toy_missing_taxa_list_with_allowed_ranges

# Convert to a data.frame for printing neatly the information
data.frame(Taxon_name = taxa_ranges$Taxon_name,
           Target_clade_name = taxa_ranges$Target_clade_name,
           Allowed_ranges = sapply(taxa_ranges$allowed_states,
                                   function(x) if (is.null(x)) "NULL"
                                               else paste(x, collapse = ", ")),
           row.names = NULL)
```

Here, the global `allowed_states` will be `c("A", "B")`.

## 1/ Which mapped range match an allowed range?

The matching rule is the only difference between the two options. For each range of the map, we list the allowed ranges that can be grafted on it, under each **matching type** option:

```{r matching}
# ------ Which allowed ranges match each range of the map? ------ #

map_ranges <- c("A", "B", "AB", "BC")
allowed <- c("A", "B", "AB", "BC")

# A range of the map matches an allowed range if it contains all of its areas
contains <- function(map_range, allowed_range)
  all(strsplit(allowed_range, "")[[1]] %in% strsplit(map_range, "")[[1]])

data.frame(Map_range = map_ranges,
           Exact_matching = map_ranges,
           Range_matching = sapply(map_ranges, function(r) 
              paste(allowed[sapply(allowed, contains, map_range = r)], collapse = ", ")),
           row.names = NULL)
```

With **exact matching** (`treat_states_as_ranges = FALSE`), a branch in `"AB"` is only available for taxa allowed in `"AB"`.

With **range matching** (`treat_states_as_ranges = TRUE`), it is also available for taxa allowed in `"A"` or `"B"`, which is accounting for a **subset sympatric speciation event**: a lineage that lived in `"AB"` can produce a descendant that lives in `"A"` only such as `(AB) -> (AB), (A)`.
Conversely, a taxon allowed in `"AB"` **cannot** be grafted on a branch in `"A"`.

When a taxon is grafted on a branch in a **larger range** than its own range, it **inherits its own allowed range**, while the branch it is grafted on continues in its range.
If several allowed ranges match, the inherited range is drawn at random among the allowed ranges **contained in the range of the branch**. Ex: a taxon allowed in `"A"` or `"B"` is grafted on branch in `"AB"`; it can inherit the range `"A"` or `"B"`, but not both.

## 2/ Check the grafting plan

`check_grafting_plan()` shows the consequences of each option **before grafting** (see `vignette("check_grafting")`):

```{r plan}
# ------ Check the plan with the two options ------ #

# Exact matching, with the global allowed ranges "A" and "B"
plan_exact <- check_grafting_plan(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges,
                                  simmap = toy_simmap_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B"),
                                  treat_states_as_ranges = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
plan_exact[, c("Taxon_name", "allowed_states", "states_available", "valid_fraction", "feasible", "cause")]

# Range matching, with the same global allowed ranges
plan_ranges <- check_grafting_plan(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges,
                                   simmap = toy_simmap_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B"),
                                   treat_states_as_ranges = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plan_ranges[, c("Taxon_name", "allowed_states", "states_available", "valid_fraction", "feasible", "cause")]
```

With exact matching, the plan flags **two problems**:

- `New_sp6` **cannot be grafted** (`cause = "allowed_states"`): its target clade is only in `"BC"`, which matches neither `"A"` nor `"B"` exactly.
- `New_sp1`, allowed in `"A"` only, has a **low valid fraction**: only 8% of the branches of its target clade are in `"A"`, so its grafting positions are concentrated on a few short branch pieces.

With range matching, `"B"` matches `"BC"` and `"A"` matches `"AB"`: all the taxa can be grafted, on a much larger share of the branches of their target clades.

## 3/ Graft with exact matching

We first graft with exact matching. The grafting stops, as `New_sp6` has no branch available:

```{r graft_exact_error}
# ------ Exact matching: infeasible plan ------ #

grafted_error <- tryCatch(
  graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges,
                     simmap = toy_simmap_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B"),
                     treat_states_as_ranges = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, seed = 1),
  error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e)))
```

With exact matching, **every range** that can be used must be listed: here, we add `"BC"` to the global `allowed_states`.

```{r graft_exact, warning = FALSE}
# ------ Exact matching: list all the ranges ------ #

grafted_exact <- graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges,
                                    simmap = toy_simmap_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B", "BC"),
                                    treat_states_as_ranges = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

## 4/ Graft with range matching

With range matching, the global `allowed_states = c("A", "B")` is enough:

```{r graft_ranges}
# ------ Range matching ------ #

grafted_ranges <- graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges,
                                     simmap = toy_simmap_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B"),
                                     treat_states_as_ranges = TRUE, verbose = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

## 5/ Compare the results

We plot the **updated stochastic maps**, in which the grafted branches are dashed, and the grafted tips are marked with a point in the color of **the range they inherited**:

```{r plot_ranges, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "100%"}
# ------ Compare the grafted phylogenies ------ #

# Helper: plot the updated simmap of a grafted phylogeny
plot_ranges <- function(phy_grafted, main)
{
  plot_grafted(phy_grafted, which = "edges", simmap_colors = range_colors, fsize = 0.55, main = main)
  grafted_tips <- which(phy_grafted$grafted_tips)
  tip_ranges <- phytools::getStates(phy_grafted$simmap, type = "tips")[phy_grafted$tip.label[grafted_tips]]
  ape::tiplabels(tip = grafted_tips, pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = range_colors[tip_ranges])
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plot_ranges(grafted_exact, main = "A: Exact matching")
plot_ranges(grafted_ranges, main = "B: Range matching")
legend("bottomleft", legend = names(range_colors), fill = range_colors, title = "Range", bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))
```

Since the grafting process is stochastic, placement can vary, and final states of taxa with multiple allowed states may vary too (e.g., `New_sp3` in `"A"` or `"B"`).
The critical change between the two matching type is the differences or not that are allowed between the range of parental branch and the inherited range of the grafted taxa.

We summarize below the **range of the branch where each taxon was grafted** (`parent_state`) and **the range it inherited** (`tip_state`) with `extract_grafting_info()`:

```{r info}
# ------ Ranges at grafting and inherited ranges ------ #

# Extract grafting information for the two matching types
info_exact <- extract_grafting_info(grafted_exact, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges)
info_ranges <- extract_grafting_info(grafted_ranges, missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges)

# Summarize information in a data.frame
compare_ranges <- data.frame(Taxon_name = info_exact$Taxon_name,
                             Exact_parent = info_exact$parent_state, Exact_inherited = info_exact$tip_state,
                             Ranges_parent = info_ranges$parent_state, Ranges_inherited = info_ranges$tip_state)
# Identify subset sympatric speciation event: the taxon inherits a range smaller than the range of the branch
compare_ranges$Ranges_subset_sympatry <- compare_ranges$Ranges_parent != compare_ranges$Ranges_inherited
compare_ranges
```

With **exact matching**, the range of the branch and the **inherited range are always the same**.

With **range matching**, taxa can be grafted on **larger ranges** and inherit a smaller one (subset sympatry), as for `New_sp2`, `New_sp4`, and `New_sp6`. 
The diversity of available positions is also wider.

## 6/ Check the grafted phylogenies

The **a posteriori** check of `check_grafting_constraints()` must use the **same `treat_states_as_ranges`** as the grafting (see `vignette("check_grafting")`):

```{r check, warning = FALSE}
# ------ A posteriori check ------ #

constraints <- check_grafting_constraints(phy_grafted = grafted_ranges, phy_backbone = toy_backbone,
                                          missing_taxa_list = taxa_ranges, allowed_states = c("A", "B"),
                                          treat_states_as_ranges = TRUE, use_excluded_subclades = FALSE,
                                          verbose = FALSE)
constraints[, c("Taxon_name", "in_tree", "target_ok", "states_ok", "ranges_ok")]
```

`states_ok` is `TRUE` when the range of the taxon is one of its allowed ranges, and `ranges_ok` when it also respects the rule of **range matching**: the branch it was grafted on contains the range it inherited.

## Next steps

Now that you know how to use **biogeographic ranges** as constraints, you may be interested in:

- combining **several traits** or a trait and ranges: `vignette("multiple_traits")`;
- exploring options to graft **missing taxa**, **missing clades**, or **both types**: `vignette("graft_missing_taxa")`, `vignette("graft_missing_clades")` and `vignette("combine_missing_taxa_and_clades")`;
- handling **uncertainty** with several simulations and stochastic maps, and ensuring the **reproducibility** of the runs with the seed system: `vignette("handle_uncertainty")`;
- speeding up your runs by using **parallel computation**: `vignette("parallel_grafting")`.
